paper_description: This paper introduces a novel approach to multiprocessor real-time scheduling that leverages hierarchical processor affinities (HPAs) to improve runtime efficiency and schedulability. It presents a strong HPA scheduler with improved time complexity for task arrivals and departures, and analyzes its performance in the context of bilevel affinity hierarchies with Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling, relating it to system optimality. The paper also details an implementation and evaluation of the proposed scheduler.

formal_description.statement: At any time t, for each ready task T_b not matched by \chi(t) and for each \Pi_j \in \alpha_b, there exists a task T_i such that (T_i, \Pi_j) \in \chi(t) and \phi_i \ge \phi_b.

formal_description.conclusion: This defines the 'Weak Invariant' for processor affinity scheduling, ensuring that if a task is not scheduled, any processor it could run on is either idle or occupied by a higher or equal priority task.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is a basic rule for processor affinity scheduling. It states that if a task cannot be scheduled on any of its allowed processors, then all of those allowed processors must be occupied by tasks that have at least as high a priority. This prevents lower-priority tasks from blocking higher-priority tasks unnecessarily.
steps: Consider a time 't'.
Identify a task 'T_b' that is ready but not currently assigned to a processor.
Look at all processors 'Pi_j' that 'T_b' is allowed to run on (i.e., 'Pi_j' is in 'T_b's affinity mask 'alpha_b').
For each such processor 'Pi_j', check if it's currently assigned to another task 'T_i'.
If 'Pi_j' is assigned to 'T_i', verify that 'T_i's priority ('phi_i') is greater than or equal to 'T_b's priority ('phi_b').
If this condition holds for all allowed processors of 'T_b', the Weak Invariant is satisfied.
key_insights: Ensures that unscheduled tasks do not block higher-priority tasks on their allowed processors.

formal_description.conclusion: This defines the 'Strong Invariant' for processor affinity scheduling, which considers task shifting. It requires that for any unscheduled task, any processor reachable via an alternating path must be occupied by a higher or equal priority task.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is a stronger condition than the Weak Invariant. It accounts for the possibility of 'task shifting' – moving tasks around to make space for others. It states that if a task 'T_b' is not scheduled, then any processor that 'T_b' could potentially reach through a sequence of alternating assignments (task-processor-task-processor...) must be occupied by a task with a priority at least as high as 'T_b's. This ensures that even with potential task movements, higher-priority tasks are not blocked by lower-priority ones.
steps: Consider a time 't'.
Identify a task 'T_b' that is ready but not currently assigned to a processor.
Determine the set 'R_b(t)' of all processors reachable from 'T_b' via alternating paths in the bipartite graph G(t) with respect to the current matching \chi(t).
For each processor '\Pi' in 'R_b(t)':
Check if '\Pi' is currently assigned to another task 'T_i' in the matching \chi(t).
If '\Pi' is assigned to 'T_i', verify that 'T_i's priority ('phi_i') is greater than or equal to 'T_b's priority ('phi_b').
If this condition holds for all reachable processors '\Pi' for 'T_b', the Strong Invariant is satisfied.
key_insights: Considers task shifting by looking at reachable processors via alternating paths.
Ensures that even with potential task movements, higher-priority tasks are not blocked by lower-priority ones.

formal_description.statement: For each i, k = 1, ..., n, either \alpha_i \subseteq \alpha_k or \alpha_k \subseteq \alpha_i or \alpha_i \cap \alpha_k = \emptyset.

variables.\\alpha_i: affinity mask of task T_i (set of allowed processors)
variables.\\alpha_k: affinity mask of task T_k (set of allowed processors)

formal_description.conclusion: This defines the property of a family of affinity masks being hierarchical (or laminar), meaning that any two affinity masks are either nested or disjoint. This structure reflects a tree-like organization of processor subsets.

informal_sketch.intuition: This definition formalizes what 'hierarchical processor affinities' means. It states that for any two tasks, their allowed sets of processors must either be completely contained within each other (one is a subset of the other) or have no overlap at all. This creates a structured, non-overlapping hierarchy, similar to how computer hardware (like caches) is organized.
steps: Consider any two tasks, T_i and T_k.
Examine their respective affinity masks, alpha_i and alpha_k.
Check if alpha_i is a subset of alpha_k.
OR check if alpha_k is a subset of alpha_i.
OR check if alpha_i and alpha_k have no common processors (their intersection is empty).
If one of these conditions is true for ALL pairs of tasks, then the affinity masks are hierarchical.
key_insights: Enforces a structured, non-overlapping hierarchy of processor sets.
Reflects hardware topology like cache levels.

Combining these, for any admitted task 'T_i' (which implies \alpha_i is considered), the set of reachable processors '\Gamma(S_i)' is exactly equal to its affinity mask '\alpha_i'.

formal_description.conclusion: This is the core of the proof for Hall's condition. It shows that the size of the reachable processor set '\Gamma(S)' is at least the size of the task set 'S', by leveraging the disjoint decomposition and the fact that each task belongs to at least one of the 'S_i' sets.

informal_sketch.intuition: This claim is the culmination of the proof for Hall's condition in Lemma III.1. It demonstrates that the number of processors available to a set of tasks 'S' ('|Gamma(S)|') is always greater than or equal to the number of tasks in 'S' ('|S|'). It achieves this by: 1) using the disjoint decomposition from the previous claim to sum the sizes of reachable processors for disjoint mask sets ('|Gamma(S_1)| + ... + |Gamma(S_q)|'), 2) applying the Hall's condition for each individual set ('|Gamma(S_i)| >= |S_i|'), 3) noting that the union of these task sets covers the original set 'S' ('|S_1 U ... U S_q| >= |S|').
steps: Start with the size of the reachable processors for set S: '|Gamma(S)|'.
Using the disjoint decomposition, this is equal to the sum of sizes of reachable processors for the disjoint mask sets: '|Gamma(S_1)| + ... + |Gamma(S_q)|'.
Apply the Hall's condition for each individual set S_i (from the previous claim): '|Gamma(S_i)| >= |S_i|'. So, the sum is >= '|S_1| + ... + |S_q|'.
Since the union of these task sets covers the original set S, the sum of their sizes is at least the size of the union: '|S_1| + ... + |S_q| >= |S_1 U ... U S_q|'.
Finally, since the union of these sets covers S, the size of the union is at least the size of S: '|S_1 U ... U S_q| >= |S|'.
Therefore, '|Gamma(S)| >= |S|'.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def prove_hall_condition_for_S(S, S_sets, Gamma_S_sets):
    # This is the core inequality derivation.
    # It relies on the previous claims and Hall's condition for individual sets.
    # |Gamma(S)| = sum(|Gamma(S_i)|)  (due to disjointness of alpha_i)
    # sum(|Gamma(S_i)|) >= sum(|S_i|) (by Hall's condition for each S_i)
    # sum(|S_i|) >= |union(S_i)| (union bound)
    # |union(S_i)| >= |S| (since S is covered by union(S_i))
    # Thus, |Gamma(S)| >= |S|
    return True # Assuming the proof holds
key_insights: Combines multiple inequalities to prove Hall's condition for any set S.
Leverages the hierarchical structure and disjoint decomposition.

formal_description.statement: The matching produced by Algorithm 2 satisfies the Strong Invariant.
formal_description.conclusion: This theorem proves that the scheduling strategy described by Algorithms 1 and 2 correctly implements strong APA scheduling, ensuring schedulability even when considering task shifting.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the main theorem of Section III.B. It proves that the assignment algorithm (Algorithm 2), when used after the admission algorithm (Algorithm 1), successfully satisfies the Strong Invariant. This means that the scheduler correctly handles processor affinities and task priorities, even when considering the possibility of moving tasks to improve scheduling.
steps: Recall the definition of the Strong Invariant (Definition II.2): for any ready task 'T_b' not matched, and for any processor '\Pi' reachable from 'T_b', there must be a higher or equal priority task assigned to '\Pi'.
The proof of this theorem relies on Lemma III.2, which states that for any unadmitted task 'T_i', the set of reachable processors 'R_i(t)' is exactly its affinity mask '\alpha_i'.
The theorem then shows two main things for any unadmitted task 'T_i':
(i) There are no alternating paths from 'T_i' to any processor outside its affinity mask '\alpha_i'.
(ii) There exists an alternating path from 'T_i' to any processor within its affinity mask '\alpha_i'.
(iii) For any task 'T_k' matched to a processor in '\alpha_i', its priority '\phi_k' is strictly greater than 'T_i's priority '\phi_i'.
(iv) No processor in '\alpha_i' is idle.
These conditions, combined with Lemma III.2, directly satisfy the requirements of the Strong Invariant.

formal_description.statement: The task set \tau is partitioned into M+1 sets \tau_0, \tau_1, ..., \tau_M and the set of processors is partitioned into M sets \pi_1, \pi_2, ..., \pi_M such that: for each T_i \in \tau_0, \alpha_i = \pi; for each i = 1, ..., M and T_k \in \tau_i, \alpha_k = \pi_i.
formal_description.conclusion: This defines a specific type of hierarchical affinity structure with two levels: tasks in \tau_0 have global affinities (can run on any processor), while tasks in \tau_i (for i>0) are restricted to a specific processor subset \pi_i.

informal_sketch.intuition: This defines a simplified, two-level structure for processor affinities. Imagine tasks are divided into two groups: a 'global' group (\tau_0) that can run anywhere, and several 'specialized' groups (\tau_1 to \tau_M) that are restricted to specific sets of processors (\pi_1 to \pi_M). This structure is common in real systems, like when some tasks are system-wide and others are tied to specific CPU clusters or NUMA nodes.
steps: Divide all tasks into M+1 groups: \tau_0, \tau_1, ..., \tau_M.
Divide all processors into M groups: \pi_1, \pi_2, ..., \pi_M.
Tasks in the first group (\tau_0) have an affinity mask that includes ALL processors (\alpha_i = \pi).
Tasks in any other group (\tau_i, where i > 0) have an affinity mask that is restricted to a specific processor group (\alpha_k = \pi_i).
key_insights: Simplifies affinity analysis to two levels.
Models common practical scenarios like global vs. clustered scheduling.

formal_description.statement: At any point in time, at least as much total work has been processed in S_infinity as in any schedule which is feasible upon platform \pi with unit-speed processors and subject to the affinity mask constraints \alpha.

variables.S_infinity: an idealized schedule using infinitely many speed-(2 - 1/m_max) processors
variables.total work processed: cumulative execution time of jobs completed

assumptions: A feasible schedule exists on m unit-speed processors.
Jobs are generated by tasks in \tau.
formal_description.conclusion: This lemma establishes a baseline for schedulability. It states that an idealized scheduler (S_infinity) using faster processors and unlimited capacity for global tasks can always process at least as much work as any feasible schedule on the actual system. This is a stepping stone to relating HPA-EDF to optimality.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma is about comparing an 'ideal' scheduler to any 'real' feasible scheduler. The ideal scheduler (S_infinity) uses faster processors (speed 2 - 1/m_max) and has unlimited capacity for the globally-scheduled tasks (\tau_0). The lemma states that this ideal scheduler will *always* process at least as much work as any scheduler that is considered feasible on the original, slower, m-processor system. This means S_infinity provides a lower bound on the work that *must* be done.
steps: Consider any schedule that is feasible on the original m unit-speed processors, respecting the affinity constraints.
Now consider the idealized schedule S_infinity.
S_infinity uses processors with speed s = 2 - 1/m_max (which is >= 1).
Crucially, S_infinity has 'infinite' capacity for tasks in \tau_0 (they can be scheduled as early as possible on dedicated extra processors).
The lemma states that at any given time, the total amount of work completed by S_infinity is greater than or equal to the total work completed by the feasible schedule.
This implies that S_infinity is a more powerful scheduler in terms of work processing capacity.

Idealized scheduler serves as a benchmark.

formal_description.statement: Consider a collection J of jobs generated by \tau and let s \ge s. Then at least one of the following holds: 1) All jobs in J are completed within their deadline under HPA-EDF on m processors of speed s, or 2) J is not feasible under the speed-s schedule S_infinity, or 3) there exists an interval I such that any feasible schedule for J must finish more than sm -2(m -1) ss s+s |I| units of work within I.

variables.HPA-EDF: Hierarchical Processor Affinities - Earliest Deadline First scheduler

assumptions: Job priorities are based on deadlines (EDF).
formal_description.conclusion: This theorem relates the performance of HPA-EDF to an idealized optimal scheduler. It states that if HPA-EDF fails to schedule a job collection J, then either J is fundamentally unschedulable even by the idealized scheduler, or the original system is extremely overloaded in a specific way within a time interval I.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is a powerful result that bounds the performance of HPA-EDF. It says that if HPA-EDF fails to schedule a set of jobs 'J' on processors of speed 's', then one of three things must be true: 1) HPA-EDF itself is the problem (it failed to schedule jobs it should have). 2) The jobs 'J' are so demanding that even an 'ideal' scheduler (S_infinity) with faster processors and unlimited global capacity cannot schedule them. 3) The jobs 'J' are so demanding that *any* feasible schedule on the original system would have to perform an extraordinary amount of work within a specific time interval 'I' to meet deadlines. This essentially means HPA-EDF is either optimal (case 1), or the system is fundamentally overloaded (cases 2 and 3).
steps: Consider a set of jobs 'J' and processors with speed 's' (where 's' is sufficiently fast).
Assume HPA-EDF fails to schedule all jobs in 'J' by their deadlines.
The theorem states that at least one of the following must be true:
a) HPA-EDF itself is the cause of the failure (meaning it's not optimal for this case).
b) The job set 'J' is so demanding that even the idealized schedule S_infinity (which uses faster processors and has unlimited global capacity) cannot schedule it.

c) The job set 'J' is so demanding that *any* feasible schedule on the original system would have to do an exceptionally large amount of work within a specific time interval 'I' to succeed. This implies a very high system load.
The bound 'sm -2(m -1) ss s+s |I|' quantifies this 'extraordinary amount of work'.
